---
format:
  revealjs:
    theme:
      - default
      - assets/theme.scss
    width: 1600
    height: 900
    # Figure-heavy science talks that need a text column beside a large figure
    # often read better on a wider canvas. To use ~21:9, set:
    #   width: 2100
    # and scale figure base_size / linewidths up to match (see the setup chunk).
    #
    # center: false keeps content top-aligned and pins the grey data-section
    # watermark to the slide bottom edge. For content-light / card decks that
    # leave a lot of empty space below the content, set `center: true` to balance
    # each slide vertically (it uses the whole slide height instead of clustering
    # at the top). Two interactions to know before flipping it: (1) the
    # data-section watermark then sits just beneath the centred content rather
    # than the slide edge, and (2) `.absolute` bleed-figure slides and
    # `.fit-narrow` assume top-aligned slides, so re-render and re-check those.
    center: false
    slide-number: c/t
    hash: true
    menu: true
    progress: true
    controls: true
    transition: fade
    embed-resources: true
    include-after-body: assets/qa-fragments.html
execute:
  echo: false
  warning: false
  message: false
params:
  config_file: "presentation.yml"
  project_root: "."
  install_missing_packages: true
---

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
# Keep embedded figures light so the self-contained HTML stays small: render
# inline figures at screen (1x) resolution. Pre-optimize any external images
# into an `optimized/` folder before embedding them (see README "File size").
# Optional sampler dependencies, named once for both installation and loading.
packages <- c(
  ragg = NA,
  systemfonts = NA
)
if (isTRUE(params$install_missing_packages)) {
  missing <- packages[
    !vapply(names(packages), requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE)
  ]
  if (length(missing)) {
    repos <- getOption("repos")
    if (is.na(repos["CRAN"]) || repos["CRAN"] == "@CRAN@") {
      repos["CRAN"] <- "https://cloud.r-project.org"
      options(repos = repos)
    }
    lib <- strsplit(Sys.getenv("R_LIBS_USER"), .Platform$path.sep)[[1]][1]
    if (!is.na(lib) && nzchar(lib)) {
      if (!dir.exists(lib)) dir.create(lib, recursive = TRUE)
      .libPaths(c(lib, .libPaths()))
    }
    options(install.packages.compile.from.source = "never")
    install.packages(names(missing))
  }
}
invisible(lapply(names(packages), function(package) {
  suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(package, character.only = TRUE))
}))

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  dev = "png",
  dev.args = list(bg = "transparent"),
  dpi = 96,
  fig.retina = 1
)
source("R/presentation_helpers.R")
dir.create("assets/generated", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
background_art_file <- "assets/generated/background-art.png"
grDevices::png(background_art_file, width = 1600, height = 900, bg = "#f7f8f5")
graphics::par(mar = rep(0, 4))
graphics::plot.new()
graphics::plot.window(xlim = c(0, 1), ylim = c(0, 1))
graphics::polygon(
  c(0, 1, 1, 0),
  c(0.00, 0.00, 0.28, 0.12),
  col = "#dcecef",
  border = NA
)
graphics::lines(
  seq(0, 1, length.out = 120),
  0.12 + 0.045 * sin(seq(0, 4 * pi, length.out = 120)),
  col = "#449bcf",
  lwd = 14
)
graphics::lines(
  seq(0, 1, length.out = 120),
  0.07 + 0.025 * cos(seq(0, 5 * pi, length.out = 120)),
  col = "#056a89",
  lwd = 7
)
grDevices::dev.off()
if (requireNamespace("ggplot2", quietly = TRUE)) {
  ggplot2::theme_set(presentation_theme())
}
cfg <- read_presentation_config(params$config_file, params$project_root)
validate_presentation_inputs(cfg)
summary_object <- load_presentation_summary(cfg)
spict <- if (identical(cfg$data$adapter, "spict")) {
  extract_spict_context(summary_object)
} else {
  NULL
}
```

## Trajectories should carry the argument {#text-figure data-section="Results"}

:::: {.text-figure}
::: {.text-panel}
- Put the interpretation beside the visual when the audience needs guidance.
- Keep the text short enough that the figure remains the dominant proof object.

::: {.takeaway}
Use `.text-figure` for concise bullets on the left and a figure on the right.
:::
:::

::: {.figure-panel}
```{r}
#| label: plot-spict-trajectories
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Charts should be generated from the compact result object. Use the analysis project for complex plotting functions and call those functions here when possible.
:::
<!-- pattern:end text-figure -->

:::: {.grid-3}
::: {.card}
::: {.card-title}

:::

`.metric-grid`

:::

::: {.card}
::: {.card-title}

:::

Use narrow tables when exact scenario values matter more than shape.
:::

This sampler slide is meant to make the reusable classes visible in the starter deck. Delete it from project decks after selecting the relevant patterns.

## Diagnostic cards keep technical checks legible {#diagnostic-grid data-section="Style sampler"}

:::: {.diagnostic-grid}
::: {.diagnostic-card}

:::

Fit

:::

2

:::

Use `.diagnostic-grid` for a short map of checks before showing dense diagnostic figures.
:::

This style works well before residual, retrospective, sensitivity, or comparison plots.

<!-- pattern:end diagnostic-grid -->

<!-- pattern:start emphasis-components -->
## Emphasis styles separate caveats from conclusions {#emphasis-components data-section="Style sampler"}

::: {.alert-box}
Use `.alert-box` for a caveat, risk, or modelling limitation that should not be missed.
:::

:::: {.takeaway-grid}
::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Finding
:::

The evidence supports one clear statement.
:::

::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Caveat
:::

The result has one important boundary.
:::

::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Next step
:::

The audience knows what to do with the result.
:::
::::

::: {.deadline}
Use `.deadline` for review dates, decision points, or meeting constraints.
:::

::: {.closing}
Use `.closing` for a short final line.
:::

::: {.notes}
Use emphasis styles sparingly. They are strongest when the rest of the slide is quiet.
:::
<!-- pattern:end emphasis-components -->

<!-- pattern:start fit-narrow -->
## A wrapped title can sit beside a full-height figure {#fit-narrow .fit-narrow data-section="Style sampler"}

::: {.fit-results}
- Put the interpretation in a narrow column on the left.
- Keep bullets brief — the figure is the proof object.
- Subscript reference points with Pandoc inline notation, e.g. B~MSY~ and F~MSY~, so they render correctly in both HTML and PDF.

::: {.fragment}
- A `.fragment` appears on the next click.
:::
:::

<!-- Replace with the real figure path. Portrait: height="1000"; landscape
     (add .fit-narrow-tight to the heading): width="950". -->
![](assets/HI_logo_farger_engelsk.png){.absolute top=-150 right=-100 height="1000"}

::: {.notes}
Use `.fit-narrow` (55 % text width) for portrait or square figures and `.fit-narrow .fit-narrow-tight` (44 %) for wide landscape figures where the content reaches further left. Place the figure with `.absolute` — e.g. `top=-150 right=-100 height="1000"` for portrait or `top=130 right=-100 width="950"` for landscape — so it bleeds past the slide margins. Put bullets in a `.fit-results` div; strong-tagged keywords pick up the `--imr-blue` colour automatically. Avoid wrapping `.fit-results` in a `.columns` grid: the `.absolute` figure floats independently of flow, so no container is needed on the text side.
:::
<!-- pattern:end fit-narrow -->

<!-- pattern:start figure-swap -->
## Swap two figures in the same spot {#figure-swap data-section="Style sampler"}

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| label: plot-swap-a
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| label: plot-swap-b
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 4.6
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::

:::

::: {.small-note}
Stack figures in a `.r-stack` and pair `.fade-out` / `.fade-in` on the same `fragment-index` to swap one figure for another in place — useful for comparing two species, scenarios, or model variants without moving the audience's eye.
:::

::: {.notes}
Both panels here draw the same placeholder; in a real deck the two chunks would plot different objects. Use `.fade-in-then-out` for the middle steps of a longer sequence so each figure appears, then clears for the next.
:::
<!-- pattern:end figure-swap -->

<!-- pattern:start figure-walkthrough -->
## Pace a multi-figure argument {#figure-walkthrough data-section="Style sampler"}

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="40%"}
Reveal one figure per click while the bullet beside it says what to look for — the text accumulates on the left, the figure swaps on the right.

**First** — establish the baseline.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
**Then** — the comparison fades in over it.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
**Finally** — land the figure you want left on screen.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| label: plot-seq-a
#| fig-width: 8.4
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1 .fade-in-then-out}
```{r}
#| label: plot-seq-b
#| fig-width: 8.4
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2 .fade-in}
```{r}
#| label: plot-seq-c
#| fig-width: 8.4
#| fig-height: 5.4
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::

:::
:::

::::

::: {.small-note}
Sync each left-column `.fragment` and its figure on the same `fragment-index`. In the `.r-stack`, the first figure is `.fade-out`, middle figures `.fade-in-then-out`, and the last `.fade-in`. With transparent figure backgrounds an earlier figure shows through later ones unless it clears itself, so every step except the last must fade out.
:::

::: {.notes}
All three chunks draw the same placeholder; in a real deck they would plot different objects (for example capability, then cost, then an effort trade-off). This is the pattern behind a text-left / figure-right walkthrough. Keep the base figure legible on its own in case the presenter skips the fragments. Chunk labels deliberately avoid the `fig-` prefix so Quarto does not add a "Figure 1" caption.
:::
<!-- pattern:end figure-walkthrough -->

<!-- pattern:start concept-hub -->
## Recreate a concept diagram in HTML/CSS {#concept-hub data-section="Style sampler"}

:::: {.text-figure}
::: {.text-panel}
- When a slide needs a simple "central thing surrounded by contributing pieces" diagram, **redraw it in HTML/CSS** rather than embedding a bitmap.
- It stays vector-crisp at any size, picks up the deck's fonts and `--imr-*` colours, and is trivial to relabel.

::: {.takeaway}
Reach for `.concept-hub` for a hub-and-spoke; reuse `.grid-3` + `.card` for a flat labelled grid. Keep bitmaps for photos and genuine external figures.
:::
:::

::: {.figure-panel}
<div class="concept-diagram">
<div class="concept-equals">System =</div>
<div class="concept-box">
<span class="concept-box-label">Boundary</span>
<div class="concept-hub-grid">
<div class="concept-sat pos-top">Input A</div>
<div class="concept-sat pos-left">Input B</div>
<div class="concept-hub">Core</div>
<div class="concept-sat pos-right">Input C</div>
<div class="concept-sat pos-bottom">Input D</div>
</div>
</div>
</div>
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
The centre sits in the middle of a 3x3 grid; add only the satellite cells you need (`pos-top`, `pos-right`, `pos-br`, `pos-bottom`, `pos-bl`, `pos-left`, `pos-tl`, `pos-tr`). Good for an assessment model and its data inputs, a stock and its sources, or any agent/harness-style anatomy. This is hand-built markup, not a generated figure — edit the divs directly.
:::
<!-- pattern:end concept-hub -->

<!-- pattern:start table-with-figure -->
## Tables can share a slide with a compact figure {#table-with-figure data-section="Style sampler"}

```{r}
#| label: table-style-sampler
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Scenario = c("Reference", "Lower catch", "Higher catch"),
    `Catch (t)` = c("TBD", "TBD", "TBD"),
    `Risk` = c("TBD", "TBD", "TBD"),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  align = c("l", "r", "r")
)
```

::: {.scenario-figure}
```{r}
#| label: plot-style-sampler
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 2.7
#| out-width: 100%
old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mar = c(2.5, 3.2, 0.4, 0.4), mgp = c(1.8, 0.6, 0))
plot(
  1:6,
  c(2.1, 2.4, 2.2, 2.8, 3.0, 3.2),
  type = "b",
  lwd = 3,
  pch = 19,
  col = "#056A89",
  xlab = "Step",
  ylab = "Relative value"
)
par(old_par)
```
:::

::: {.notes}
Use `.scenario-figure` when a narrow table needs a small visual check beneath it. Keep the figure compact so the table remains readable.
:::
<!-- pattern:end table-with-figure -->

<!-- pattern:start wide-figure -->
## Give a dense figure two-thirds of the slide {#wide-figure data-section="Style sampler"}

::: {.text-figure .figure-wide-right}
::: {.text-panel}
- Use this variant when axis labels, facets, or uncertainty bands need more width.
- Keep the interpretation to two or three short bullets.

::: {.takeaway}
Widen the proof object before shrinking it.
:::
:::

::: {.figure-panel}
```{r}
#| label: plot-wide-figure
#| fig-width: 9.2
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| out-width: 100%
plot_spict_trajectories(spict)
```
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Add `.figure-wide-right` to `.text-figure` when the chart needs roughly two-thirds of the slide. If the figure still feels crowded, remove text rather than reducing labels below the presentation minimum.
:::
<!-- pattern:end wide-figure -->

<!-- pattern:start map-layout -->
## Maps need room for geography and context {#map-layout data-section="Style sampler"}

::: {.text-figure .map-slide}
::: {.text-panel}
- State why location changes the interpretation.
- Keep the legend short and the mapped area uncluttered.

::: {.takeaway}
Use `.map-slide` when text and geography need balanced weight.
:::
:::

::: {.figure-panel}
```{r}
#| label: plot-map-layout
#| fig-width: 7.2
#| fig-height: 5.3
#| out-width: 100%
old_par <- graphics::par(no.readonly = TRUE)
graphics::par(mar = c(1.2, 1.2, 0.5, 0.5), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i")
graphics::plot.new()
graphics::plot.window(xlim = c(0, 10), ylim = c(0, 8), asp = 1)
graphics::polygon(c(0.3, 3.1, 4.2, 2.4, 0.4), c(0.3, 0.8, 3.2, 6.9, 7.6), col = "#d6dedb", border = "#667985", lwd = 2)
graphics::polygon(c(7.0, 9.8, 9.8, 8.1, 6.6), c(0.4, 0.4, 7.7, 6.1, 2.8), col = "#e7ece8", border = "#667985", lwd = 2)
graphics::points(c(4.8, 5.6, 6.1, 5.2), c(2.1, 3.7, 5.4, 6.4), pch = 21, bg = "#d44f56", col = "white", cex = 2.2, lwd = 2)
graphics::text(5.4, 0.8, "Survey stations", col = "#173042", cex = 1.2)
graphics::par(old_par)
```
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The `.map-slide` modifier gives the text and map near-equal width. Use `.figure-wide-right` instead when the geographic proof should dominate.
:::
<!-- pattern:end map-layout -->

<!-- pattern:start absolute-figure -->
## Let one scientific figure reach the slide edge {#absolute-figure data-section="Style sampler"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="34%"}
- Use a normal RevealJS column for the interpretation.
- Place the dominant figure inside the wide column.
- Apply `.absolute` to the figure output, not to unrelated text.

::: {.takeaway}
This is the supported escape hatch for figure-heavy science slides.
:::
:::

::: {.column width="66%"}
```{r}
#| label: plot-absolute-figure
#| classes: absolute
#| fig-width: 9.4
#| fig-height: 5.6
#| out-width: 105%
x <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 80)
graphics::plot(x, 0.35 + 0.5 * x + 0.07 * sin(10 * x), type = "l", lwd = 5, col = "#056a89", xlab = "Time", ylab = "Relative index", bty = "l")
graphics::polygon(c(x, rev(x)), c(0.29 + 0.5 * x, rev(0.41 + 0.5 * x)), col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#449bcf", 0.2), border = NA)
graphics::lines(x, 0.35 + 0.5 * x + 0.07 * sin(10 * x), lwd = 5, col = "#056a89")
```
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
Pair RevealJS `.columns` with an `.absolute` figure in the wide column. Reserve arbitrary freehand positions for true hero images and small decorative accents.
:::
<!-- pattern:end absolute-figure -->

<!-- pattern:start background-art -->
## Decorative art can sit behind the message {#background-art .background-art background-image="assets/generated/background-art.png" background-size="cover" background-position="center"}

::: {.background-copy}
::: {.title-kicker}
Background image
:::

::: {.title-heading}
Keep decoration behind the message.
:::

::: {.title-subtitle}
Use a slide background for wide artwork so the graphic spans the canvas and never sits on top of the text.
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
A `background-image` is preferable to an absolute image chunk for edge-to-edge decorative graphics. The capture workflow must discover this slide even though Reveal inserts `data-background-*` attributes into its section tag.
:::
<!-- pattern:end background-art -->

<!-- pattern:start custom-font -->
## Bundle occasional hand-drawn annotations {#custom-font .custom-font-demo data-section="Style sampler"}

::: {.text-figure}
::: {.text-panel}
- Keep the font file under `assets/fonts/`.
- Register it with `systemfonts`.
- Render with `ragg`, not the default quartz PNG device.

::: {.takeaway}
The deck stays self-contained with no system font installation.
:::
:::

::: {.figure-panel}
```{r}
#| label: plot-custom-font
#| dev: ragg_png
#| fig-width: 7.4
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| out-width: 100%
family <- register_xkcd_font()
graphics::plot(c(0, 1), c(0, 1), type = "n", axes = FALSE, xlab = "", ylab = "")
graphics::arrows(0.16, 0.28, 0.78, 0.72, length = 0.12, lwd = 4, col = "#056a89")
graphics::text(0.48, 0.48, "Explain the jump", family = family, cex = 2.1, col = "#d44f56", srt = 12)
graphics::points(0.82, 0.75, pch = 21, bg = "#6ca67a", col = "white", cex = 3, lwd = 2)
```
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
The bundled TTF is the only binary font asset that must stay versioned. The `ragg_png` device honours `systemfonts::register_font()`; the default macOS quartz PNG device does not.
:::
<!-- pattern:end custom-font -->

<!-- pattern:start table-variants -->
## Use named table sizes before shrinking text {#table-variants data-section="Style sampler"}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="49%"}
### Medium table

::: {.table-medium}
```{r}
#| label: table-medium-demo
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Scenario = c("Reference", "Lower", "Upper"),
    Catch = c(780, 720, 840),
    Interpretation = c("Central case", "Lower pressure", "Higher pressure")
  ),
  align = c("l", "r", "l")
)
```
:::
:::

::: {.column width="49%"}
### Tight table

::: {.table-tight}
```{r}
#| label: table-tight-demo
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    Year = 2024:2026,
    A = c(1.02, 1.04, 1.05),
    B = c(0.91, 0.95, 0.98),
    C = c(0.84, 0.88, 0.92),
    D = c(1.12, 1.09, 1.06),
    E = c(0.76, 0.79, 0.82)
  ),
  digits = 2
)
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.takeaway}
If a named size is still too small, move columns to the appendix.
:::

::: {.notes}
Use `.table-medium` for a mid-width table with an explanation column and `.table-tight` for a genuinely wide table. Neither class authorizes unreadably dense content.
:::
<!-- pattern:end table-variants -->

<!-- pattern:start scenario-table -->
## Compare scenarios in one table {#scenario-table data-section="Results"}

::: {.table-medium}
```{r}
#| label: scenario-table
knitr::kable(
  scenario_table(spict),
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r")
)
```
:::

::: {.takeaway}
State the decision-facing comparison in one sentence.
:::

::: {.notes}
Keep tables narrow enough to read from the back of the room. Put the full scenario table in an appendix if more columns are needed.
:::
<!-- pattern:end scenario-table -->

<!-- pattern:start takeaway-grid -->
## End with what should stick {#takeaway-grid data-section="Close"}

:::: {.takeaway-grid}
::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Finding
:::

State the most important empirical result.
:::

::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Interpretation
:::

Explain why that result matters.
:::

::: {.takeaway-card}
::: {.card-title}
Next action
:::

Ask for the discussion, decision, or follow-up you need.
:::
::::

::: {.fragment .fade-in .closing-inline}
Thank you — questions and discussion
:::

::: {.notes}
Do not end on a generic thank-you slide. End on the message the audience should remember. The `.closing-inline` fragment fades in on the presenter's last click, so the conclusions boxes are the resting state and the sign-off appears only when the presenter is ready to invite questions.
:::
<!-- pattern:end takeaway-grid -->
